competitors.description: A softness-descending confidence mixer: Linha-Fina (trained statistical classifier) leads at high, Palavreado (order-independent keyword bag, no learning) backs it at medium, Nebulento (fuzzy string matching, the loosest/most tolerant of the three) closes at low.
competitors.notes: HYPOTHESIS: unlike trident (three-tier but engines picked for architectural distinctness), cascade-soft is picked for a deliberately monotonic 'strictness' gradient — trained classifier (least tolerant of paraphrase, most precise) -> rigid-but-vocab-flexible keyword bag -> fuzzy matcher (most tolerant of ASR noise/typos, least precise) — to test whether ordering engines by how loosely they match, not just by paradigm, is itself a useful axis distinct from trident's paradigm-diversity axis. Linha-Fina is a template-paradigm statistical classifier (see ENGINE_REGISTRY: 'linha_fina.opm:LinhaFinaPipeline', paradigm='template') distinct from both Jurebes (sklearn baseline family) and Padatious (neural+exact-gate), so this fighter and trident do not test the same top stage. exact_match not applicable to linha-fina/palavreado/nebulento (jurebes-only config key, verified absent from linha_fina/opm.py and palavreado/opm.py's self.config.get(...) call sites).

competitors.description: Four distinct paradigms, one engine each, staggered by tier: Padatious (neural template, exact matches included via its own internal padaos gate) leads, Adapt (keyword rules) backs it at high, then Palavreado (keyword bag) and Nebulento (fuzzy template) share medium recall, with Adapt low as the final catch-all.
competitors.notes: HYPOTHESIS: does a maximal-diversity cascade (one stage per paradigm, no paradigm repeated) beat curated 2-3 engine pairs? Slimmed from the original 7-stage config: dropped the explicit Padacioso-high stage because Padatious already runs padaos internally (disable_padaos=false) and returns conf=1.0 for perfect/regex matches before its neural score is even consulted, so a separate padacioso stage tested nothing padatious wasn't already doing; dropped the redundant padatious-medium retry since a second tier of the same trained classifier is not an independent paradigm and wasn't separately justified.

competitors.description: Second embedding-fronted fighter, a paradigm sibling of m2v-first with a different embedding-space strategy: Hierarchical-KNN (nearest-neighbour search over an embedding index, coarse-to-fine domain-then-intent routing) leads at high, Linha-Fina's trained statistical classifier backs it at medium.
competitors.notes: HYPOTHESIS: m2v-first tests a flat single-vector-similarity embedding front door; knn-first tests a structurally different embedding mechanism — nearest-neighbour retrieval over a (documented hierarchical: domain-then-intent) index, config-verified in ovos_hierarchical_knn_pipeline/__init__.py (conf_high/conf_medium/conf_low, index_dir, hf repo id default) rather than a single learned classifier boundary. Pairing it with Linha-Fina (not Padatious, already used by m2v-first) keeps the two embedding-fronted fighters from sharing a backup engine, so a head-to-head between them isolates the embedding-front difference rather than being confounded by which classifier backs each up. Both m2v (dense sentence embeddings) and hierarchical-knn (KNN retrieval over an embedding index) are 'embeddings' paradigm per ENGINE_REGISTRY import paths (ovos_m2v_pipeline / ovos_hierarchical_knn_pipeline), distinct from every trained-classifier or keyword-rule engine used elsewhere in the league.

competitors.description: Replacement-family sibling: Palavreado (order-independent bag-of-keywords) fills the keyword-high slot, Padatious backs it up at medium — identical shape and backup to mycroft-classic, which stands in for the Adapt side of this A/B.
competitors.notes: FAMILY: kw-slot A/B — mycroft-classic (adapt-high -> padatious-medium) vs kw-slot-palavreado (palavreado-high -> padatious-medium). There is no separate kw-slot-adapt fighter: that config is identical to mycroft-classic (adapt-high -> padatious-medium), and per the 1-fighter-per-config rule mycroft-classic itself now serves as the 'keyword engine = adapt' side of this A/B rather than duplicating the same pipeline under a second competitor_id. This sibling swaps only the keyword-high engine (Palavreado in for Adapt); backup engine and tier (padatious-medium) held fixed against mycroft-classic. Isolates whether Adapt's stricter ordered require/optional grammar or Palavreado's looser order-independent bag-of-keywords matching makes a better front-door gate ahead of an identical Padatious backstop.

competitors.description: The first embedding-fronted fighter in the league: Model2Vec sentence-embedding similarity leads at high confidence, Padatious's trained template classifier backs it at medium.
competitors.notes: HYPOTHESIS: none of the existing fighters (frankenparse, padapt, nebulatious, nebulapt, palavadapt) use embeddings at all — every stage in every prior fighter is either keyword-rule matching or a trained-per-intent template classifier. m2v-first tests whether leading with a general-purpose sentence-embedding similarity engine (Model2Vec, config-verified in ovos_m2v_pipeline/__init__.py: model default 'Jarbas/ovos-model2vec-intents-distiluse-base-multilingual-cased-v2', conf_high/conf_medium/conf_low keys) — which generalizes across paraphrases via embedding distance rather than exact template/keyword matching — beats a template classifier leading, when Padatious backs it up at medium. This isolates 'does an embedding-similarity front door change which utterances get caught first' from every non-embedding fusion already in the league. Distinct paradigm from Jurebes/Padatious (learned per-intent classifiers over hand-engineered or TF-IDF features) and from Nebulento (fuzzy string edit-distance, not vector similarity).

competitors.description: The historical Mycroft-AI intent order, before OVOS restructured the pipeline into confidence-interleaved stages: Adapt is the primary keyword-rule parser, Padatious runs only as a fallback after Adapt fails to match anything.
competitors.notes: SOURCE: mycroft-core PR #939 ('Implement Padatious support (examples based intent parser)', MatthewScholefield) added Padatious to mycroft-core by making PadatiousService inherit from FallbackSkill (per forslund's review comment 'Make PadatiousService inherit from FallbackSkill to fix new fallback changes' on that PR) — i.e. Padatious was wired in as a fallback handler invoked only when Adapt's IntentBuilder grammar produced no match, not as a co-equal parallel matcher. Author confirmed back-compat ('Adapt will still work :)'). This is the inverse of the modern OVOS/mycroft-dev order (see ovos-stock.json and current MycroftAI/mycroft-core dev intent_service.py, which interleaves padatious-high ahead of adapt) — the point of this fighter is to test whether that later re-ordering (template-first) actually helped, by running the original adapt-first/padatious-fallback shape through the arena. Modeled as adapt-high -> padatious-medium: Adapt gets first shot at its own high gate; Padatious's medium tier (not high) reflects that classic Padatious ran as a general-purpose fallback rather than a first-look high-confidence matcher. Arena skips: fallback-skill priority tiers (90-99 catch-all range documented in Mycroft's Fallback Skill docs) don't exist as an arena stage — Padatious substitutes directly for 'the fallback', consistent with the historical mechanism. SHARED BASELINE ROLE: this exact pipeline (adapt-high -> padatious-medium) is also the natural 'keyword engine = adapt' / 'template engine = padatious' cell of both replacement-study grids below — rather than keep separate duplicate-config fighters (kw-slot-adapt, tmpl-slot-padatious) alongside this one (1 fighter per config, no exceptions), mycroft-classic itself now serves as that shared baseline for both families: kw-slot family compares mycroft-classic against kw-slot-palavreado (keyword-engine A/B, Padatious backup+shape fixed); tmpl-slot family compares mycroft-classic against tmpl-slot-{nebulento,linhafina,jurebes} (template-engine 4-way, Adapt front+shape fixed). Its historical framing and its role as the shared adapt/padatious baseline are not in tension — the config is the same regardless of which question is being asked of it.

competitors.description: Nebulento × Adapt fusion — precise keyword rules take the first shot, fuzzy matching mops up typos and ASR noise, and Adapt medium catches the remainder.
competitors.notes: HYPOTHESIS: does a strict keyword-rule engine (Adapt, low false-positive but brittle to phrasing/typos) at high confidence, backstopped by a fuzzy keyword matcher (Nebulento, tolerant of ASR noise and near-misses) at medium, and a lower-bar Adapt retry, beat either engine alone? Adapt and Nebulento are different matching strategies (strict rule vs fuzzy), so this tests real precision/recall complementarity, not a duplicate.

competitors.description: Padatious × Nebulento fusion — the neural parser leads at high confidence, fuzzy string matching mops up typos and ASR noise, neural medium catches the rest.
competitors.notes: HYPOTHESIS: does a neural template classifier (Padatious) at high confidence, backed by a fuzzy template matcher (Nebulento) tuned for typos/ASR noise, beat either alone — and does retrying Padatious at a looser gate afterward recover cases the fuzzy stage still missed? Padatious's internal padaos exact-match gate already covers regex-perfect input (verified in ovos_padatious/intent_container.py), so this pair specifically probes the neural-vs-fuzzy paraphrase gap, not exact-match duplication.

competitors.description: The real shipped ovos-core default intent pipeline, reproduced faithfully with the arena's available plugins: Padatious high, Adapt high, m2v (Model2Vec embedding) high, Adapt medium.
competitors.notes: SOURCE: the exact shipped order, verbatim, from the installed ovos-config package's default mycroft.conf — /home/miro/.venvs/ovos/lib/python3.12/site-packages/ovos_config/mycroft.conf, 'intents.pipeline' key, lines 218-231 (ovos-config==<installed version>): ["ovos-stop-pipeline-plugin-high", "ovos-converse-pipeline-plugin", "ovos-ocp-pipeline-plugin-high", "ovos-padatious-pipeline-plugin-high", "ovos-adapt-pipeline-plugin-high", "ovos-m2v-pipeline-high", "ovos-ocp-pipeline-plugin-medium", "ovos-fallback-pipeline-plugin-high", "ovos-stop-pipeline-plugin-medium", "ovos-adapt-pipeline-plugin-medium", "ovos-fallback-pipeline-plugin-medium", "ovos-fallback-pipeline-plugin-low"]. SKIPS (arena cannot instantiate these outside a full ovos-core session — no skill-service converse loop, no OCP media-skill roster, no fallback-skill registry): ovos-stop-pipeline-plugin-{high,medium} (requires a running skill with stop handlers), ovos-converse-pipeline-plugin (requires active-skill session state), ovos-ocp-pipeline-plugin-{high,medium} (requires OCP media skills registered), ovos-fallback-pipeline-plugin-{high,medium,low} (requires fallback-skill registrations; nothing left to fall back to in the intent-only benchmark). What remains — padatious-high, adapt-high, m2v-high, adapt-medium — is exactly the intent-classifier subset of the stock order, in stock order, so this fighter is the arena's best-effort faithful reproduction of 'what ovos-core actually ships', not a curated fusion hypothesis. m2v-pipeline config keys verified in ovos_m2v_pipeline/__init__.py: conf_high (default 0.7), conf_medium (default 0.5, note the plugin uses 'conf_medium' not 'conf_med'), conf_low (default 0.15).

competitors.description: Replacement-family member: Adapt fixed at keyword-high, Jurebes (sklearn MLP classifier, the top-accuracy baseline on the intents-for-eval en-US template board) fills the template-medium slot.
competitors.notes: FAMILY: tmpl-slot 4-way — mycroft-classic (adapt-high -> padatious-medium) is the shared baseline; siblings are tmpl-slot-nebulento, tmpl-slot-linhafina, tmpl-slot-jurebes (this file), each swapping only the template-medium engine with adapt-high held fixed. There is no separate tmpl-slot-padatious fighter: that config is identical to mycroft-classic, and per the 1-fighter-per-config rule mycroft-classic itself serves as the 'template engine = padatious' cell of this grid rather than duplicating the same pipeline under a second competitor_id. This sibling swaps in Jurebes using the same top-accuracy 'mlp_shallow' baseline selected for trident.json (accuracy 0.8154 on frontend-static/public/data/benchmark-intent_template-intents-for-eval-en-US.json among all jurebes-* entries), with exact_match forced to false so the fighter tests the trained classifier itself rather than jurebes's own internal exact-template short-circuit — consistent with the exact_match:false convention used everywhere jurebes appears in this pass. adapt-high held fixed as the front door, matching the other tmpl-slot siblings.

competitors.description: Replacement-family member: Adapt fixed at keyword-high, Linha-Fina (trained statistical template classifier) fills the template-medium slot.
competitors.notes: FAMILY: tmpl-slot 4-way — mycroft-classic (adapt-high -> padatious-medium) is the shared baseline; siblings are tmpl-slot-nebulento, tmpl-slot-linhafina (this file), tmpl-slot-jurebes, each swapping only the template-medium engine with adapt-high held fixed. There is no separate tmpl-slot-padatious fighter: that config is identical to mycroft-classic, and per the 1-fighter-per-config rule mycroft-classic itself serves as the 'template engine = padatious' cell of this grid rather than duplicating the same pipeline under a second competitor_id. This sibling swaps in Linha-Fina, a distinct trained-classifier engine from Padatious and Jurebes (see ENGINE_REGISTRY import path 'linha_fina.opm:LinhaFinaPipeline'), with adapt-high held fixed as the front door. Never previously paired with plain Adapt in the registry (linha-fina does not appear in frankenparse/padapt/nebulatious/nebulapt/palavadapt), so this is the first head-to-head data point for Linha-Fina against the keyword-rule paradigm specifically.

competitors.description: Replacement-family member: Adapt fixed at keyword-high, Nebulento (fuzzy string matching over templates) fills the template-medium slot.
competitors.notes: FAMILY: tmpl-slot 4-way — mycroft-classic (adapt-high -> padatious-medium) is the shared baseline; siblings are tmpl-slot-nebulento (this file), tmpl-slot-linhafina, tmpl-slot-jurebes, each swapping only the template-medium engine with adapt-high held fixed. There is no separate tmpl-slot-padatious fighter: that config is identical to mycroft-classic, and per the 1-fighter-per-config rule mycroft-classic itself serves as the 'template engine = padatious' cell of this grid rather than duplicating the same pipeline under a second competitor_id. This sibling swaps in Nebulento (fuzzy edit-distance-style template matching, tolerant of typos/ASR noise) as the backup, with adapt-high held fixed. Note this pipeline shape (adapt-high -> nebulento-medium -> [no third stage]) is a strict 2-stage subset of nebulapt.json's 3-stage adapt-high -> nebulento-medium -> adapt-medium; kept as a separate, deliberately shorter fighter because the family's isolation question is 'first successful replacement per engine' with no retry stage, whereas nebulapt additionally tests whether an adapt-medium retry recovers more on top of the pair — a different, additive hypothesis.

competitors.description: A three-tier confidence mixer across three genuinely distinct template paradigms: Padatious (learned template similarity + internal exact-match gate) at high, Jurebes (sklearn MLP classifier over TF-IDF features, the top-accuracy baseline on the intents-for-eval en-US template board) at medium, Nebulento (fuzzy string matching) as the loosest low-confidence catch-all.
competitors.notes: HYPOTHESIS: does mixing three architecturally distinct classifiers by descending confidence tier — neural-template-with-exact-gate (Padatious) high, statistical-ML classifier (Jurebes) medium, fuzzy-string (Nebulento) low — beat any two-engine fusion in the league? Unlike frankenparse (which mixes paradigms but stays single-tier-per-engine at similar confidence bands), trident deliberately spans the full high/medium/low ladder with one engine per rung, so it also probes whether a strict confidence-descending cascade (not just paradigm diversity) is itself a useful shape. BASELINE SELECTION: 'mlp_shallow' is the top-accuracy entry on frontend-static/public/data/benchmark-intent_template-intents-for-eval-en-US.json among all jurebes-* competitor_ids (accuracy 0.8154, beating jurebes-sgd-modified-huber at 0.8143 and every other of the ~55 published jurebes sklearn baselines on that board). Config key verified in jurebes/opm.py (self.baseline = self.config.get('baseline', 'linear_svc')) and jurebes/baselines.py ('mlp_shallow': lambda: _p(tfidf_word(), MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(64,), max_iter=500))). exact_match set to false per spec (jurebes/opm.py: self.exact_match = bool(self.config.get('exact_match', True)) — forced off here so this fighter tests the trained MLP classifier itself, not jurebes's own internal exact-template short-circuit, which would otherwise duplicate what Padatious's high-tier stage already does one step earlier in the cascade).

competitors.description: Domain-partitioned variant of Adapt: registered vocabulary and intents are grouped by skill_id into a per-skill IntentDeterminationEngine per language; inference runs every per-skill engine and returns the global argmax. Same distribution and confidence gate as adapt-medium, registered under a separate opm.pipeline entry point (DomainAdaptPipeline in ovos_adapt/opm.py).
competitors.notes: Single-stage pipeline at the plugin's own medium-confidence gate; per-plugin config keeps the same documented thresholds as adapt-medium. This variant is parallel (every domain engine scores, then argmax), not gated two-stage routing. Hypothesis: should improve precision over the flat pipeline on large multi-domain intent sets by keeping decision boundaries local to each skill's vocabulary, and be roughly neutral on small single-domain sets.

competitors.description: Two-stage variant of Adapt: vocabulary and intents are filed under a domain == skill_id, a top-level classifier picks the domain first, then only that domain's sub-engine matches the intent. Same distribution and confidence gate as adapt-medium, registered under a separate opm.pipeline entry point (HierarchicalAdaptPipeline in ovos_adapt/opm.py).
competitors.notes: Same medium-confidence gate and thresholds as adapt-medium; isolates the two-stage routing shape from the flat pipeline. Hypothesis: domain-first routing should help precision on large multi-domain intent sets by rejecting cross-domain keyword near-misses before they compete, and be roughly neutral-to-worse on small single-domain sets where there is no domain structure to exploit.

competitors.description: Classic rule-based keyword intent parser from the Mycroft era: intents are built from required and optional vocabulary groups, matched by keyword presence regardless of word order.
competitors.notes: Single-stage pipeline at the plugin's own medium-confidence gate; per-plugin config keeps the shipped defaults.

competitors.description: Two-stage variant of Palavreado: intents are filed under a domain == skill_id, a top-level classifier picks the domain first, then only that domain's sub-container keyword-matches the intent. competitors.description: Two-stage hierarchical k-NN over a pre-built FAISS IVF+PQ index of IBM Granite multilingual embeddings: domain-level search scoped to loaded skills, then intent-level scoring with Wu-Lin pairwise probability estimation.

competitors.description: Domain-partitioned variant of Linha Fina: intents are grouped by skill_id into per-skill SVM engines held in one DomainIntentEngine per language; inference runs every per-skill engine in parallel and returns the global argmax. Same distribution and confidence gate as linha-fina-medium, registered under a separate opm.pipeline entry point (DomainLinhaFinaPipeline in linha_fina/opm.py).
competitors.notes: Single-stage pipeline at the plugin's own medium-confidence gate; the per-plugin config pins the same documented thresholds as linha-fina-medium. This variant is parallel (every domain engine scores, then argmax), not gated two-stage routing like the hierarchical variant — hypothesis: should improve precision over the flat pipeline on large multi-domain intent sets by keeping decision boundaries local to each skill's vocabulary, and be roughly neutral on small single-domain sets. KNOWN BROKEN as of linha-fina 0.3.0a1: LinhaFinaPipeline.handle_initial_train (linha_fina/opm.py:138) calls self.containers[lang].train(), but DomainLinhaFinaPipeline's containers are DomainIntentEngine instances which have no .train() method (AttributeError on 'mycroft.ready') -- confirmed by a live train/match sanity run in this PR. Needs an upstream fix in linha-fina before this fighter can produce real predictions; kept in the registry so a fix is picked up automatically.

competitors.description: Two-stage variant of Linha Fina: intents are partitioned by skill_id, a top-level classifier maps the query to a single skill_id first, and only that skill's per-intent SVM engine resolves the intent. Same distribution and confidence gate as linha-fina-medium, registered under a separate opm.pipeline entry point (HierarchicalLinhaFinaPipeline in linha_fina/hierarchical_opm.py). Needs at least 2 domains and 3 intents globally before either stage can train (the plugin's own constraint).
competitors.notes: Same medium-confidence gate and thresholds as linha-fina-medium; 'domain_threshold': 0.0 keeps the top-level domain gate disabled (shipped default) so the comparison isolates the two-stage routing shape from linha-fina-domain-medium's parallel-argmax shape. Hypothesis: domain-first gating should help precision on large multi-domain sets by rejecting cross-domain queries before any sub-engine scores, and be weaker or equal on small single-domain sets where the domain classifier has too little signal to train reliably. KNOWN BROKEN as of linha-fina 0.3.0a1: LinhaFinaPipeline.handle_initial_train (linha_fina/opm.py:138) calls self.containers[lang].train(), but HierarchicalLinhaFinaPipeline's containers are HierarchicalIntentEngine instances which have no .train() method (AttributeError on 'mycroft.ready') -- confirmed by a live train/match sanity run in this PR. Needs an upstream fix in linha-fina before this fighter can produce real predictions; kept in the registry so a fix is picked up automatically.

competitors.description: Trains one SVM per intent over one-hot keyword vectors, selecting the most relevant negative samples by fuzzy token-set ratio. Entities come from simplematch templates and wordlists.
competitors.notes: Single-stage pipeline at the plugin's own medium-confidence gate; the per-plugin config pins the documented confidence thresholds. The engine itself is fixed: one SVM per intent over one-hot keyword vectors.

competitors.description: Classifies utterances with a pretrained Model2Vec static-embedding intent classifier restricted to intents registered by loaded skills. The default model is multilingual, distilled from LaBSE.
competitors.notes: Single-stage pipeline at the plugin's own medium-confidence gate; per-plugin config keeps the shipped defaults. Published predictions are migrated from the legacy ovos-intent-benchmark, where this engine was trained on the benchmark's own corpora; the pinned pretrained model targets real OVOS skill intents and cannot emit this benchmark's label space, so native re-sweeps require a dataset-trained variant.

competitors.description: Domain-grouped variant of Markov: each intent is grouped under a domain == skill_id (from the 'skill_id:intent' label), and inference first routes the utterance to a domain via DomainMarkovIntentEngine, then resolves the intent inside it by lowest perplexity. Same distribution and confidence gate as markov-medium, registered under a separate opm.pipeline entry point (DomainMarkovPipeline in ovos_markov_pipeline/__init__.py).
competitors.model: order-2 word-level Markov chains, Kneser-Ney smoothing with backoff, domain-grouped
competitors.notes: Same medium-confidence gate and model parameters as markov-medium; the per-plugin config pins the same n-gram order, smoothing, backoff, stemming, char fallback and confidence thresholds so the comparison isolates domain-first routing. Hypothesis: routing to a domain before scoring perplexity within it should help precision on large multi-domain intent sets (chains from other skills stop competing), and be roughly neutral-to-worse on small single-domain sets where the domain stage adds overhead without payoff.

competitors.description: Trains one word-level Markov chain per intent from example utterances and picks the intent whose chain yields the lowest perplexity; confidence is derived from perplexity. Trains in milliseconds with no GPU.
competitors.model: order-2 word-level Markov chains, Kneser-Ney smoothing with backoff
competitors.notes: Single-stage pipeline at the plugin's own medium-confidence gate; the per-plugin config pins the documented model parameters (n-gram order, smoothing, backoff, stemming, char fallback) and confidence thresholds.

competitors.description: Two-stage variant of Nebulento: intents are filed under a domain == skill_id, a top-level classifier picks the domain first, then only that domain's sub-container fuzzy-matches the intent. Same nebulento distribution and confidence gate as nebulento-medium, registered under a separate opm.pipeline entry point (HierarchicalNebulentoPipeline in nebulento/opm.py).
competitors.notes: Same medium-confidence gate and thresholds as nebulento-medium; 'domain_threshold': 0.0 keeps the top-level domain gate disabled (matches the shipped default) so the comparison isolates the two-stage routing shape. Hypothesis: domain-first routing should help precision on large multi-domain intent sets by rejecting cross-domain fuzzy near-misses before they compete, and be roughly neutral-to-worse on small single-domain sets where there is no domain structure to exploit.

competitors.description: Fuzzy-matching intent engine: compares utterances against example sentences with string-similarity ratios instead of exact rules, trading precision for resilience to typos and ASR noise.
competitors.notes: Single-stage pipeline at the plugin's own medium-confidence gate; per-plugin config keeps the shipped defaults.

competitors.description: Deterministic, regex-based drop-in replacement for Padatious. No training step and no false positives on unseen phrasings — what you template is exactly what you match.
competitors.notes: Single-stage pipeline at the plugin's own medium-confidence gate; per-plugin config keeps the shipped defaults.

competitors.description: Same Padatious engine as padatious-medium, with the plugin's own two-stage DomainIntentContainer switched on via 'domain_engine': true: utterances first route to a skill_id-scoped domain container, then match against that domain's intents only.
competitors.notes: Same plugin id and medium-confidence gate as padatious-medium; the only config change is flipping 'domain_engine' from false to true, which swaps the internal IntentContainer for DomainIntentContainer (ovos_padatious/domain_container.py). Hypothesis: domain-first two-stage routing should help precision on large multi-domain intent sets (fewer cross-domain false positives) at the cost of an extra routing step, and be roughly neutral-to-worse on small single-domain sets where there is no domain structure to exploit.

competitors.description: Lightweight neural intent parser trained on expanded example sentences. The OVOS default intent engine: fast to train, fast to match, tolerant to small variations in phrasing.

competitors.notes: Plugin default model; CUDA optional via 'use_cuda'. Langs pinned to the language set actually exercised in scoring (Whisper is auto-detect/multilingual by design, but an empty langs list made this fighter eligible against every board rather than only the ones it was evaluated on).

competitors.description: Whisper decoding fused with a KenLM n-gram language model via whisper-lm-transformers. This fighter pairs a Basque fine-tuned Whisper medium checkpoint with the HiTZ Basque 5-gram LM.
competitors.notes: README reference configuration; lm_alpha/lm_beta are the published optimized values for Basque.

competitors.description: OpenAI Whisper base model running on whisper.cpp, a dependency-free C/C++ inference engine optimized for CPU (AVX, Arm Neon, mixed F16/F32).
competitors.notes: Plugin default model; ggml weights auto-downloaded on first load. Langs pinned to the language set actually exercised in scoring (Whisper is auto-detect/multilingual by design, but an empty langs list made this fighter eligible against every board rather than only the ones it was evaluated on).

competitors.description: OpenAI Whisper small model running on whisper.cpp, a dependency-free C/C++ inference engine optimized for CPU (AVX, Arm Neon, mixed F16/F32).
competitors.notes: Size-tier variant of whispercpp-base: same plugin defaults, one size up; ggml weights auto-downloaded on first load. Langs pinned to the language set actually exercised in scoring (Whisper is auto-detect/multilingual by design, but an empty langs list made this fighter eligible against every board rather than only the ones it was evaluated on).

competitors.description: Wraps AhoTTS from the Aholab group, a concatenative synthesizer with linguistic processing for Basque and Spanish.
competitors.notes: README reference configuration with Basque selected.

competitors.description: Renders letters, digits and punctuation as R2D2-style droid beeps by concatenating bundled sound files. Produces signalling sounds rather than speech.
competitors.notes: Shipped defaults: r2d2 voice, bundled droid sound bank.

competitors.description: Coqui TTS running the English VITS model trained on LJSpeech, an end-to-end neural synthesizer combining a variational autoencoder with adversarial training.
competitors.notes: Pretrained model id from the plugin README model list; sibling entry points cover XTTS, FreeVC and Fairseq MMS variants.

competitors.description: Unit-selection synthesizer for Galician (also usable for Spanish) that concatenates prerecorded segments, selecting among parallel intonation contours. The default sabela voice balances quality and speed.
competitors.notes: Requires the cotovia Debian packages (executable plus gl/es linguistic data).

competitors.description: Uses the Microsoft Edge read-aloud service via the edge-tts library; no account required. The full Edge neural voice catalog, including multilingual voices, is selectable by voice name.
competitors.notes: README reference configuration with the en-US-AriaNeural voice.

competitors.description: Wraps the espeak-ng command-line synthesizer, a compact formant-synthesis engine covering over 100 languages and accents. This fighter runs the f1 female voice variant on US English.
competitors.notes: Voice-variant fighter complementing espeakng-m1: same engine and language, female variant appended to the language code (en-us+f1). Requires the espeak-ng binary on the system.

competitors.description: Wraps the espeak-ng command-line synthesizer, a compact formant-synthesis engine covering over 100 languages and accents. This fighter runs the m1 male voice variant on US English.
competitors.notes: README reference configuration; requires the espeak-ng binary on the system. The voice variant is appended to the language code (en-us+m1).

competitors.description: The Google Translate read-aloud voice via the gTTS library; no account required. The British English accent is selected with the co.uk top-level domain.
competitors.notes: Same plugin as google-tx-en-us under a different tld — a distinct competitor (US vs UK accent).

competitors.description: Synthesizes through the undocumented Google Translate speech endpoint via gTTS, pinned to the US English accent via the tld option.
competitors.notes: lang/tld pair from the plugin's documented REGIONAL_CONFIGS map for en-US. The README warns this endpoint is unofficial and unsuitable for production or commercial use.

competitors.description: LuxTTS, a lightweight zipvoice-based voice-cloning TTS (>150x realtime). Clones the voice in the reference clip pointed at by prompt_audio.
competitors.notes: Voice-cloning fighter — set prompt_audio to a reference clip; a different reference voice is a different competitor. TTS ranks by human votes only.

competitors.description: Client for a MaryTTS server (or MaryTTS-compatible APIs such as OpenTTS and Larynx); the server synthesizes with hidden semi-Markov model and unit-selection voices.
competitors.notes: Requires a separately hosted MaryTTS server; README reference configuration.

competitors.description: Wraps the Mimic 1 binary, a flite-based concatenative synthesizer; voices are festvox flitevox files loadable from paths or URLs.
competitors.notes: Requires the mimic binary; README reference configuration with the ap voice.

competitors.description: Zero-shot multilingual (600+ language) TTS from the k2-fsa/sherpa/icefall team, run locally via the omnivoice/torch runtime. Supports voice cloning (ref_audio), free-text voice design (instruct), or letting the model pick a speaker automatically ('auto', used here). Arabic is first-class, with 22 regional varieties as distinct lang tags.
competitors.notes: Runs a local multi-GB model (CPU or CUDA, auto-detected); no API key or remote server required, unlike the Azure/Google cloud TTS fighters. GPU strongly recommended for real-time synthesis; 'lazy' loading is the plugin default so config-only validation does not require the weights.

competitors.description: Wraps the SVOX Pico engine (nanotts, pico2wave or pico-tts binaries), a tiny offline synthesizer with six built-in voices. This fighter runs the en-US voice.
competitors.notes: Voice pinned to en-US from the README's documented voice list; requires a pico binary (nanotts/pico2wave/pico-tts) on the system.

competitors.description: Software Automatic Mouth, a rule-based formant synthesizer producing retro 8-bit robotic English speech. Voice presets are pitch/throat/mouth/speed parameter sets fed to the sam binary.
competitors.notes: Compiles and installs the sam binary on first run when not found system-wide.

competitors.description: The classic energy/denoise VAD extracted from the old ovos-listener: speech is audio whose max/current energy ratio falls below a threshold. No model, CPU-only.
competitors.notes: Energy-based VAD; the ratio/energy thresholds are config. A different threshold is a different competitor on the false-accept / false-reject curve.

competitors.description: Energy/denoise VAD at a higher max/current ratio threshold (3.0) — calls more audio speech than the 2.0 default (lower false-reject, higher false-accept).
competitors.notes: Threshold variant of noise-vad — a different ratio threshold is a different competitor.

competitors.description: A tiny recurrent (precise-lite) TFLite VAD trained with precise-lite-trainer on a mix of wake-word and non-wake-word audio (Common Voice, ESC-50, UrbanSound8K, FSD50K, AudioSet, and community wake-word data), run at its plugin default threshold.
competitors.notes: Baseline at the plugin's default threshold (0.35). The flat key is read by the listener's VAD manager and the nested key is read by the plugin itself, matching the other VAD fighters' key-duplication convention. A -thr03/-thr07-style threshold variant can follow once this baseline is on a board.

competitors.description: Silero neural voice-activity detector running on a small ONNX model; the listener's default VAD. Robust to music and environmental noise.
competitors.notes: Single VAD fighter at the plugin's own threshold; speech decision is 'any voiced frame in the clip'.

competitors.description: Silero VAD at a sensitive 0.3 threshold — calls more audio speech (lower false-reject, higher false-accept) than the 0.5 default.
competitors.notes: Threshold variant: a different threshold is a different competitor on the false-accept / false-reject curve.

competitors.description: Silero VAD at a strict 0.7 threshold — calls less audio speech (lower false-accept, higher false-reject) than the 0.5 default.
competitors.notes: Threshold variant: a different threshold is a different competitor on the false-accept / false-reject curve.

competitors.description: The classic WebRTC energy/GMM voice-activity detector. Tiny, CPU-only and fast; aggressiveness 0-3 trades false-accepts against false-rejects (3 = most aggressive at rejecting non-speech).
competitors.notes: Single VAD fighter; vad_mode pins the aggressiveness. A different vad_mode is a different competitor.

competitors.description: WebRTC VAD at aggressiveness 1 — less aggressive at rejecting non-speech than mode 3 (lower false-reject, higher false-accept).
competitors.notes: Config variant: a different aggressiveness (vad_mode) is a different competitor on the false-accept / false-reject curve.

competitors.description: microWakeWord streaming TFLite model for 'hey jarvis' (the tiny inception-style network used on ESP32 devices), auto-downloaded from the official ESPHome model repository.
competitors.notes: ESPHome publishes models for a fixed phrase set (okay_nabu, hey_jarvis, alexa, …); 'hey mycroft' is not among them.

competitors.description: microWakeWord 'hey jarvis' fronted by a Silero pre-wake VAD gate: the detector only runs on clips the VAD calls speech.
competitors.notes: Combo fighter: wake-word engine + pre-wake VAD. The same engine without the VAD, or with a different VAD, is a different competitor.

competitors.display_name: microWakeWord + Silero VAD + speaker verifier (hey jarvis)
competitors.description: The full listener stack for 'hey jarvis' on microWakeWord: a Silero pre-wake VAD gate, then the microWakeWord detector, then a speaker-verification confirm.
competitors.notes: Combo fighter: pre-wake VAD + wake-word engine + verifier. Each distinct (engine, VAD, verifier) triple is its own competitor.

competitors.description: microWakeWord 'hey jarvis' followed by a speaker-verification gate: an activation only counts when the verifier confirms it.
competitors.notes: Combo fighter: wake-word engine + verifier. The same engine without the verifier is a different competitor.

competitors.description: microWakeWord streaming TFLite model for 'hey jarvis' (the tiny inception-style network used on ESP32 devices), auto-downloaded from the official ESPHome model repository.
competitors.notes: Threshold variant of microwakeword-hey-jarvis: probability_cutoff raised from the plugin default 0.5 to 0.7, trading recall for fewer false activations. Same ESPHome hey_jarvis.tflite model.
Pretrained openWakeWord 'alexa' model.

competitors.description: openWakeWord running its pretrained 'hey jarvis' model on a shared mel-spectrogram + embedding frontend; streams 80 ms frames and scores each against the activation threshold.
competitors.notes: Pretrained model auto-selected by hotword name.

competitors.description: openWakeWord models running on a shared mel-spectrogram and embedding frontend. The pretrained model matching the hotword name is loaded automatically, here the bundled hey_mycroft model.
competitors.notes: Pretrained model auto-selected by hotword name; threshold is the plugin default.

competitors.description: openWakeWord 'hey mycroft' fronted by a Silero pre-wake VAD gate: the detector only runs on clips the VAD calls speech, suppressing false-accepts on music and noise at the risk of missing very quiet speech.
competitors.notes: Combo fighter: wake-word engine + pre-wake VAD. The same engine without the VAD, or with a different VAD, is a different competitor.

competitors.notes: Combo fighter: pre-wake VAD + wake-word engine + verifier. Each distinct (engine, VAD, verifier) triple is its own competitor.

competitors.description: openWakeWord 'hey mycroft' followed by a speaker-verification gate: an activation only counts when the verifier confirms it, trading a small false-reject increase for fewer false-accepts.
competitors.notes: Combo fighter: wake-word engine + verifier. The same engine without the verifier is a different competitor.

competitors.description: openWakeWord 'hey mycroft' at a sensitive 0.3 activation threshold — more activations (lower false-reject, higher false-accept) than the 0.5 default.
competitors.notes: Threshold variant: a different threshold is a different competitor — it lands a different point on the false-accept / false-reject curve and battles as its own entry.

competitors.description: openWakeWord 'hey mycroft' at a strict 0.7 activation threshold — fewer activations (lower false-accept, higher false-reject) than the 0.5 default.
competitors.notes: Threshold variant: a different threshold is a different competitor — it lands a different point on the false-accept / false-reject curve and battles as its own entry.

competitors.display_name: wakeforge + Silero VAD + speaker verifier (hey jarvis)
competitors.description: The full listener stack for 'hey jarvis' on wakeforge: a Silero pre-wake VAD gate, then the wakeforge featurizer+classifier, then a speaker-verification confirm.
competitors.notes: Combo fighter: pre-wake VAD + wake-word engine + verifier. Each distinct (engine, VAD, verifier) triple is its own competitor.

competitors.description: wakeforge 'hey jarvis' followed by a speaker-verification gate: an activation only counts when the verifier confirms it.
competitors.notes: Combo fighter: wake-word engine + verifier. The same engine without the verifier is a different competitor.

competitors.description: wakewordlab pretrained 'hey jarvis' model on a shared mel/embedding frontend with an optional Silero VAD pre-filter; models are auto-downloaded by name and cached.
competitors.notes: Pretrained model selected by name; threshold and the built-in VAD pre-filter are config. A different model/threshold is a different competitor. The VAD gate (config.hotwords.hey_jarvis.vad / vad_threshold) is built into the plugin's own config block, not a separate listener.VAD pipeline stage — do not expect a listener.VAD block when diffing this against the openWakeWord -silero combo fighters.

competitors.description: wakewordlab 'hey jarvis' fronted by an external Silero pre-wake VAD gate (the plugin's own built-in VAD is disabled to avoid double-gating).
competitors.notes: Combo fighter: wake-word engine + pre-wake VAD. The plugin's own config.hotwords.hey_jarvis.vad is set to false and an external listener.VAD stage is used instead, so this gate is the same mechanism as the openWakeWord -silero combo fighters (vs. the bare wakewordlab-hey-jarvis fighter, which uses the plugin's built-in VAD gate).

competitors.description: The full listener stack for 'hey jarvis' on wakewordlab: an external Silero pre-wake VAD gate (the plugin's own built-in VAD is disabled to avoid double-gating), then the wakewordlab detector, then a speaker-verification confirm.
competitors.notes: Combo fighter: pre-wake VAD + wake-word engine + verifier. The plugin's own config.hotwords.hey_jarvis.vad is set to false and an external listener.VAD stage is used instead, so this gate is the same mechanism as the openWakeWord -silero combo fighters (vs. the bare wakewordlab-hey-jarvis fighter, which uses the plugin's built-in VAD gate).

competitors.description: wakewordlab 'hey jarvis' followed by a speaker-verification gate: an activation only counts when the verifier confirms it. The plugin's own built-in VAD gate is disabled (vad:false) for this fighter.
competitors.notes: Combo fighter: wake-word engine + verifier. The plugin's own config.hotwords.hey_jarvis.vad is set to false here so the verifier is isolated from the built-in VAD gate; compare against the bare wakewordlab-hey-jarvis fighter (built-in VAD on, no verifier).

competitors.description: wakewordlab 'hey jarvis' at a strict 0.7 threshold — fewer activations (lower false-accept, higher false-reject) than the 0.5 default.
competitors.notes: Threshold variant of wakewordlab-hey-jarvis. The VAD gate (config.hotwords.hey_jarvis.vad / vad_threshold) is built into the plugin's own config block, not a separate listener.VAD pipeline stage — do not expect a listener.VAD block when diffing this against the openWakeWord -silero combo fighters.

competitors.description: Delegates wake-word detection to a shared remote host over a persistent WebSocket connection (satellite architecture): streams raw PCM frames to the server and receives detection events back, instead of running any model locally.
competitors.notes: Remote-dependent, like the Azure/Google cloud fighters: requires a reachable ovos-ww-plugin-server host (default ws://localhost:8338); optional 'api_key' config sends 'Authorization: Bearer <key>'. No local model weights. Streams raw PCM frames but is not tagged 'stream' capability here since that tag is reserved by tests/test_ww_stream.py for the openwakeword-/microwakeword-/precise-onnx- families.
